title: Killing duality for a split rational root decomposition
statement: Let $L$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple $\mathbf Q$-Lie algebra [def-wf-lie-algebra, def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra]. Let $H\subseteq L$ be a maximal abelian subalgebra acting diagonally over $\mathbf Q$, with $L=H\oplus\bigoplus_{\rho\in R}L_\rho$, where $R\subset H^\vee\setminus\{0\}$ is its reduced crystallographic root system, $L_\rho=\{x:[h,x]=\rho(h)x\text{ for all }h\in H\}$ is one-dimensional, and $h_\rho\in[L_\rho,L_{-\rho}]\subseteq H$ is characterized by $\rho(h_\rho)=2$. Define $B(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}_L(\operatorname{ad}(x)\operatorname{ad}(y))$, using ordinary trace [def-weil-endomorphism-trace]. Then $B$ is symmetric and invariant: $B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z])$. Its restriction to $H$ is positive definite over $\mathbf Q$, meaning $B(h,h)>0$ for $h\ne0$. Consequently for each $\lambda\in H^\vee$ there is a unique $t_\lambda\in H$ satisfying $B(t_\lambda,h)=\lambda(h)$ for all $h\in H$. The symmetric bilinear form $b(\lambda,\mu)=B(t_\lambda,t_\mu)$ on $H^\vee$ is positive definite and satisfies $b(s_\rho\lambda,s_\rho\mu)=b(\lambda,\mu)$ for $s_\rho(\lambda)=\lambda-\lambda(h_\rho)\rho$. For every $\rho\in R$, put $d_\rho=b(\rho,\rho)$. Then $d_\rho>0$, $h_\rho=2t_\rho/d_\rho$, and for every $x\in L_\rho$, $y\in L_{-\rho}$ one has $[x,y]=B(x,y)t_\rho$.

proof.text: In any basis of $L$, the trace definition gives $\operatorname{tr}(AC)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}C_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(CA)$ by exchanging $i,j$. It also gives linearity in each matrix. Since $\operatorname{ad}$ is linear, $B$ is bilinear; taking $A=\operatorname{ad}x$, $C=\operatorname{ad}y$ proves symmetry.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: Write $A=\operatorname{ad}x$, $C=\operatorname{ad}y$, $D=\operatorname{ad}z$. Jacobi gives $\operatorname{ad}[x,y]=AC-CA$. The cyclic trace identity of step 1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(CAD)=\operatorname{tr}(ADC)$, by applying it to $C$ and $AD$. Thus $B([x,y],z)=\operatorname{tr}(ACD-CAD)=\operatorname{tr}(A(CD-DC))=B(x,[y,z])$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: Choose a basis of $H$ together with one nonzero vector in each one-dimensional $L_\rho$; the assumed direct sum makes this a basis of $L$. For $h,k\in H$, the product $\operatorname{ad}h\operatorname{ad}k$ is zero on $H$ and multiplication by $\rho(h)\rho(k)$ on $L_\rho$. Reading its diagonal yields $B(h,k)=\sum_{\rho\in R}\rho(h)\rho(k)$, in particular $B(h,h)=\sum_{\rho\in R}\rho(h)^2\geq0$ in $\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: If every $\rho(h)=0$, then $[h,H]=0$ and $[h,L_\rho]=0$ for every root, hence $[h,L]=0$ by the direct sum. The line $\mathbf Qh$ is then a solvable ideal: $[L,\mathbf Qh]=0$ and $[\mathbf Qh,\mathbf Qh]=0$. Semisimplicity forces $h=0$. Thus for nonzero $h$ some summand in step 3 is strictly positive; all others are nonnegative, so $B(h,h)>0$. In particular $B|_H$ is nondegenerate in both variables: vanishing against every vector implies vanishing against itself.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: Apply the finite-dimensional perfect-pairing lemma with $K=\mathbf Q$, $M=N=H$ and $p=B|_H$, whose two separation hypotheses were proved in step 4. The map $\Phi:H\to H^\vee$, $v\mapsto B(v,-)$ is a linear isomorphism. Set $t_\lambda=\Phi^{-1}(\lambda)$; this proves the required existence and uniqueness and makes $\lambda\mapsto t_\lambda$ linear. Consequently $b(\lambda,\mu)=B(t_\lambda,t_\mu)$ is symmetric bilinear. If $\lambda\ne0$, then $t_\lambda\ne0$, so $b(\lambda,\lambda)>0$ by step 4.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: For $x\in L_\rho$, $y\in L_{-\rho}$ and $h\in H$, Jacobi gives $[h,[x,y]]=[[h,x],y]+[x,[h,y]]=\rho(h)[x,y]-\rho(h)[x,y]=0$. The common zero eigenspace is exactly $H$: in the assumed decomposition a component in $L_\sigma$ annihilated by every $h$ vanishes, since $\sigma\ne0$ allows an $h$ with $\sigma(h)\ne0$. Hence $[x,y]\in H$. Invariance now gives $B([x,y],h)=B(x,[y,h])=\rho(h)B(x,y)=B(B(x,y)t_\rho,h)$. Nondegeneracy on $H$ yields $[x,y]=B(x,y)t_\rho$.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: Step 6 and bilinearity show $[L_\rho,L_{-\rho}]\subseteq\mathbf Qt_\rho$: this bracket of subspaces means the span of their brackets. Hence the given $h_\rho$ equals $c t_\rho$ for a rational $c$. As $\rho\ne0$, step 5 gives $d_\rho=b(\rho,\rho)>0$, and $\rho(t_\rho)=B(t_\rho,t_\rho)=d_\rho$. Evaluating $\rho(h_\rho)=2$ gives $c=2/d_\rho$, proving the claimed formula without division by zero.

source.place: Section 23h, printed pp.503,508 (PDF pp.515,520): split decomposition and coroot normalization; agent calculation from these explicit hypotheses.

proof.text: By symmetry and duality, $b(\lambda,\rho)=B(t_\lambda,t_\rho)=\lambda(t_\rho)$. Step 7 therefore gives $\lambda(h_\rho)=2b(\lambda,\rho)/d_\rho$. Put $a=b(\lambda,\rho)$, $c=b(\mu,\rho)$ and $d=d_\rho$. Expanding by bilinearity, $b(s_\rho\lambda,s_\rho\mu)=b(\lambda,\mu)-2ac/d-2ac/d+4ac d/d^2=b(\lambda,\mu)$, as $d>0$. This proves reflection invariance for all $\lambda,\mu$, including zero.
